title: Mitochondrial Myopathies: CPEO vs. Kearns-Sayre Syndrome
summary: A high-yield clinical overview of the spectrum of mitochondrial ocular myopathies, ranging from isolated Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) to the life-threatening systemic triad of Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS). This guide covers the genetic basis, diagnostic workup, and critical cardiac monitoring requirements.

sections.title: Clinical Definitions
sections.content: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) is characterized by slow, progressive, bilateral, non-fatigable ptosis followed by symmetrical restriction of all extraocular movements. When CPEO is associated with multisystem involvement including pigmentary retinopathy, onset before age 20, and cardiac conduction defects, it is classified as Kearns-Sayre Syndrome (KSS).

branches: Single large-scale mtDNA deletions (most common in KSS)
Nuclear DNA mutations affecting mtDNA maintenance (POLG1, PEO1, SLC25A4)
Heteroplasmy: Ratio of mutant to wild-type mtDNA determines severity
High metabolic demand tissues (Extraocular muscles, Retina, Heart) affected first

content.explanation: MUST have all three: 1. Onset < 20 years old. 2. CPEO (Ptosis + Ophthalmoplegia). 3. Pigmentary Retinopathy (Salt-and-pepper). PLUS at least one of: Cardiac conduction block, CSF protein >100mg/dL, or Cerebellar Ataxia.

rows: Slowly progressive, bilateral, symmetrical. Often the first sign.
Severe, early onset. Significant levator function loss.
Symmetrical restriction in all gazes. No diplopia (usually).
Spared, though retinopathy may affect visual fields.
Reduced Bell's phenomenon; risk of neurotrophic keratitis.
Fatigability, variability, diurnal fluctuation, Cogan's lid twitch, Ice test (+).
Autosomal Dominant, onset in 5th-6th decade, dysphagia, limb-girdle weakness.
Lid retraction (vs ptosis), proptosis, restrictive strabismus on forced duction.
Acute onset, ataxia, areflexia, post-viral, GQ1b antibodies (+).
Present from birth, lid lag on downgaze, poor levator function.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Clinical History & Exam (Evaluate for ptosis symmetry and diplopia presence).
Step 2: Cardiology Referral (MANDATORY EKG/Holter to rule out heart block).
Step 3: Blood/Urine Testing (Lactate, Pyruvate, Creatine Kinase levels).
Step 4: Genetic Testing (Targeted mtDNA deletion/point mutation analysis via blood/saliva).
Step 5: Lumbar Puncture (If KSS suspected: evaluate for CSF protein > 100 mg/dL).
Step 6: Muscle Biopsy (Gold standard if genetics inconclusive: Gomori Trichrome staining for 'Ragged Red Fibers').

sections.title: Lethal Warning Signs
content: Syncope or Dizziness (Potential Mobitz II or 3rd-degree heart block)
Sudden cardiac death risk in KSS (requires pacemaker)
Severe Dysphagia (Aspiration risk in CPEO+ syndromes)
Acute corneal ulceration post-ptosis surgery (Absent Bell's)

sections.title: Histopathology & Microscopy
content: Ragged Red Fibers (RRF): Subsarcolemmal accumulation of abnormal mitochondria (Gomori Trichrome).
COX-Negative Fibers: Cytochrome c oxidase deficiency in specific muscle fibers.
Electron Microscopy: 'Parking lot' crystalline inclusions (paracrystalline).
Succinate Dehydrogenase (SDH) staining: Hyper-reactive 'blue' fibers.

sections.title: Management Strategies
content: Conservative: Ptosis crutches on glasses, prisms (rarely needed).
Ptosis Surgery: Frontalis suspension (Sling) is preferred over levator resection.
Surgical Caution: Under-correct ptosis to prevent exposure keratopathy.
Medical: Coenzyme Q10 (120-160mg/day) and L-Carnitine (limited evidence).
Cardiac: Prophylactic pacemaker placement for KSS with any conduction delay.

content.explanation: S: Sling (Frontalis), T: Tension-free, A: Avoid overcorrection, Y: Yield to poor Bell's, S: Silicone rods (reversible), A: Artificial tears, F: Frequent follow-up, E: Exposure check.

sections.title: Recent Advances & Landmark Studies
content: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy (MRT): 'Three-parent baby' techniques for prevention.
Gene Editing: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) to shift heteroplasmy in vitro.
Study: Zeviani et al. (1988) first established the link between mtDNA deletions and KSS/CPEO.
Nadir et al. (2023): Investigating Elamipretide for mitochondrial stabilization.

sections.title: Epidemiology at a Glance
content: Prevalence: ~1.6 per 100,000 for all mitochondrial diseases.
Gender: No predilection; affects males and females equally.
Onset CPEO: Typically 18-40 years.
Onset KSS: Strictly < 20 years (usually first decade).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Because EOM restriction is symmetrical, patients rarely complain of diplopia; they simply turn their heads.
CPEO is the most common manifestation of mitochondrial disease in adults.
Always check for orbicularis weakness (often present in CPEO, mimicking MG).
The pigmentary retinopathy of KSS is often asymptomatic and doesn't usually cause significant vision loss, unlike Retinitis Pigmentosa.
A negative muscle biopsy does NOT rule out CPEO if only one muscle group was sampled (mosaic distribution).
